title: Arjuna drops his bow
hook: the greatest archer's hands shake and his bow slips, Krishna answers with karmany eva, and the Hindu habit of offering the work
carry: karma yoga: do the work, offer it to Krishna
tomorrow: Jagannath means lord of the world. so why does he leave his temple?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a proud son came home, and his father answered with tat tvam asi: atman and Brahman, one, or two. Today, a line from the Gita that most people only know in translation, and the shaking hands it was spoken to.

Feel it in the body first. The mouth goes dry. The legs go weak. The skin burns. The hair stands up on the arms. That's how the Bhagavad Gita describes Arjuna, the greatest archer of his age, standing between two armies, looking across at teachers and cousins he's about to fight. His bow, Gandiva, slips out of his hand. He sits down in his chariot. He says he won't fight. And Krishna, driving his chariot, starts to answer.
screen: `DRY MOUTH. WEAK LEGS.` → `THE BOW SLIPS.` → `HE SITS DOWN.`

segments.voice: In chapter two, Krishna gives him one of the most quoted lines in the Gita. It opens: karmany eva. A dictionary won't list karmany. That's sandhi: undo the join. Karmani, in action, ends in i. Eva, alone, begins with e. Before a different vowel, the mouth slides the i into a y, and Sanskrit writes the slide down. Karmani eva: in action alone. The whole line: your right is to action alone, never to its fruit. Don't let the fruit be your motive, and don't fall in love with doing nothing either. This is karma yoga, the yoga of action. It isn't don't care. Arjuna still has to pick up the bow and do his duty, his dharma, fully. What he lets go of is his grip on how it turns out. And later the Gita takes it one step further: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you give, Krishna says, do it as an offering to me. That's why, in many Hindu homes, especially in the south, people finish a task, a meal, a prayer, with three words: Sri Krishnarpanam astu. May this be offered to Krishna. The work is yours. The fruit is his. Many teachers read Arjuna's story this way: the hands steady once the outcome is no longer yours to carry.
screen: `KARMANI + EVA: IN ACTION ALONE.` · `NEVER TO ITS FRUIT.` · `NOT 'DON'T CARE.' DO IT FULLY.` · `SRI KRISHNARPANAM ASTU.` · then, large: `DO THE WORK. OFFER IT TO KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: Notice where your body is holding a result you're waiting for: a tight jaw, a knot in the stomach, shoulders up. Name the task behind it. Now do what Arjuna was asked to do: give it your full effort in your mind, then set the outcome down. If you pray, say quietly, Sri Krishnarpanam astu. If you don't, say, the work is mine, the result isn't. Let the shoulders drop, and breathe.
Sandhi plainly: today, i turning into y before a different vowel, so karmani eva, in action alone, comes out karmany eva.
For the road: karma yoga. Do the work, offer it to Krishna. Arjuna picked up the bow again. See you tomorrow.

fork.reveal: karma yoga: your right is to the action, never to the fruit, and not to doing nothing. Arjuna still fights; he lets go of the outcome, and offers the work to Krishna.

original.note: Sanskrit: karmaṇy evādhikāras te, your right is to action alone; Bhagavad Gita 2.47. karmaṇi + eva, with the i turned into y.

notes: Written fresh for year 5 (Sanskrit for readers, 'sandhi plainly'). Takes i/u becoming y/v before an unlike vowel.
Ashtadhyayi 6.1.77 (iko yaṇ aci) cited; the script says only i and u, though the rule also covers ṛ and ḷ.
Bhagavad Gita 2.47 opening paraphrased in English and given in transliteration only, as a sandhi example.
